newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa sees special sugar trade deal in region.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa sees special sugar trade deal in region.

text.p: Southern Africa's sugar industry will have to be accommodated in a special regional trade deal to avert conflict between countries in the region, Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin said.
The sugar industries of South Africa and Swaziland are currently locked in a sugar trade war, with the South Africans cutting off research and other aid, leaving the Swazis pondering retaliation.
"There can be no merit whatsoever in different countries trying to advance their sugar industries at the expense of others. It is a cul-de-sac, it won't work," Erwin told Reuters.
Erwin said Pretoria had been in touch with the South African Sugar Association (SASA) and the Swazi government on the spat.

SASA said last year it would would cut Swaziland off from using the export terminal in Durban and also refused Swazi access to research and training facilities, claiming that imports of cheaper Swazi sugar cost the local industry up to 275 million rand a year.
The Swaziland Sugar Association says its policy is not to sell sugar directly into the South African market and blames rogue traders for the sales.

But Erwin said sugar would have to be accommodated under a special protocol in a future free trade agreement in the Southern African Development Community (SADC), of which both Swaziland and South Africa were members.
"The sugar industry as a whole in SADC, in our view, will have to be placed within some special protocol within the (free trade) agreement," he said in an interview late on Tuesday.

The South African industry dwarfs that of Swaziland and expects output of almost 2.4 million tonnes this year (April to March). The kingdom expects around 460,000 tonnes of sugar during its production year.

South Africa will have around one million tonnes of sugar for export. Swaziland expects to send around 200,000 tonnes to the U.S. and the European Union under preferential sugar quotas at prices of up to three times the prevailing world market price.

Erwin said it was not up to the South African government to regulate relations between the two sugar industries but added, "It is our job to try and ensure that the overall arrangement with regard to sugar is effective and equitable".
"The harsh reality is that we as SADC member states must address the matter of sugar. If we don't, all will be losers, none will be gainers".
